problems.title: Spectral objectives differ
claim: The author-released implementation optimizes the printed spectral objective.
analysis: The current paper penalizes adjacent predicted-band differences \(\|D\widehat r\|^2\), whereas forward_loss penalizes \(\|D(\widehat r-r)\|^2\). For ten-band perfect reconstruction \(r=\widehat r=(0,1,1,\ldots,1)\), all values lie in the allowed range, yet the printed penalty is \(1\) and the released penalty is \(0\). Mean rather than sum reduction changes a positive factor, not this zero-set discrepancy. In a two-band analytic slice with squared reconstruction plus weight \(0.25\), the printed objective has optimum \((1/6,5/6)\), while the error-difference objective is zero at \((0,1)\). This slice demonstrates distinct objectives, not a full-network optimum. The current defaults also differ from the printed weights. Historical training effects remain unknown.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Reconcile the specific equation, reported quantity or source contract described above. Corrected full-experiment results remain unverified.

problems.title: Balanced macro-F1 need not equal accuracy
claim: Balanced single-label datasets have macro-F1 equal to accuracy.
analysis: The balanced confusion matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}100&0\\50&50\end{pmatrix}\) has accuracy \(0.75\) but macro-F1 \((0.8+2/3)/2\simeq0.733333\). Balanced classes therefore do not imply macro-F1 equals accuracy. Standard micro-F1 equals accuracy for single-label classification; the paper's EuroSAT entries need their actual aggregation specified.

problems.title: A directional cap is not energy conservation
claim: The directional output cap enforces energy conservation in the claimed general sense.
analysis: A reciprocal BRDF equal to one inside a \(30^\circ\) polar cap and zero outside has hemispheric reflectance \(\pi/4<1\), but a directional reflectance factor \(\pi>1.2\). Thus an imposed directional cap can be a useful heuristic without being equivalent to energy conservation.

problems.title: Channel smoothing and wavelength-derivative energy are distinct scopes
claim: The printed adjacent-band difference is a spectral smoothness regularizer.
analysis: For unequal center-wavelength gaps, a piecewise-linear approximation to integrated squared derivative is \[\int |r\prime(\lambda)|^2\,d\lambda\approx\sum_b\frac{(r_{b+1}-r_b)^2}{\lambda_{b+1}-\lambda_b}.\] The printed unweighted differences instead define a valid regularizer on channel adjacency. Section 3.1 motivates smoothness in wavelength but does not assert equality to this particular derivative integral. Band-response integration and real spectral edges further bound the physical interpretation. This distinguishes quantities without demonstrating that the chosen regularizer is invalid or empirically inferior.
result: The channel regularizer is mathematically legitimate. The observation limits a stronger continuous-wavelength interpretation and supplies no separate model-error finding.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
problems.impact_rationale: A valid channel-adjacency prior need not equal a wavelength-derivative integral; the paper does not establish that stronger equality.
problems.existing_correction_status: No mathematical repair is required for using the stated channel regularizer; the physical interpretation remains bounded.
